title: Can an NRI Be the Sole Trustee of an Indian Private Trust?
excerpt: Indian trust law creates significant hurdles for NRIs seeking sole trusteeship, from residency requirements under the Indian Trusts Act to FEMA restrictions on property-holding trusts.
body:
• Section 60 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, bars persons domiciled outside India from serving as trustees of Indian resident trusts.
  • Section 73 allows replacement of a trustee who is absent from India for six continuous months or leaves to reside abroad.
  • The ITAT has ruled that NRIs can serve as trustees of valid Indian trusts — but at least one resident trustee is advisable.
  • FEMA regulations add a separate layer of restrictions, particularly for trusts holding immovable property in India.

For NRIs managing family wealth back in India, creating a private trust is one of the most common estate planning tools. But a critical question trips up many families: can an NRI serve as the sole trustee of an Indian private trust? The short answer is that Indian law makes it extremely difficult, and in practice, having at least one India-resident trustee is nearly always necessary.

What the Indian Trusts Act Says

The Indian Trusts Act of 1882 governs private trusts in India. While it does not contain an outright ban on NRI trustees, two provisions create serious obstacles.

Section 60, Explanation 1, states that a person domiciled abroad or an alien enemy is "not a proper person to be a trustee" of an Indian resident trust. Indian courts have interpreted this to mean that a non-resident cannot serve as trustee unless they are domiciled in India. The legal reasoning is straightforward: a trustee must remain within the jurisdiction of Indian courts to ensure the terms of the trust can be enforced.

Section 73 provides that if a trustee is absent from India for a continuous period of six months, or leaves India for the purpose of residing abroad, a new trustee may be appointed in their place by the person nominated in the trust deed. This effectively creates an automatic replacement mechanism that undermines any NRI's ability to maintain long-term sole trusteeship.

"Indian courts have held that a non-resident cannot be a trustee of an Indian resident trust unless he is domiciled in India."

— TaxGuru legal analysis

The ITAT Exception

The picture is not entirely one-sided. The New Delhi bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), in Global Academy of Emergency Medicine v. CIT(E), held that appointing NRIs as trustees of valid Indian trusts is permissible under the Income Tax Act. In that case, the CIT(E) had rejected a trust's registration application because all five trustees were NRIs with foreign citizenship. The ITAT overturned the decision, noting that one trustee was domiciled in India and that the presence of NRI trustees alone did not invalidate the trust.

The key takeaway: the ITAT upheld the trust, but the case still had at least one India-domiciled trustee. A trust with exclusively NRI trustees remains vulnerable to challenge.

FEMA Adds Another Layer

The Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) creates additional restrictions. Under India's exchange control regime, a trust holding immovable property cannot have a non-resident as its sole trustee. FEMA regulations govern how NRIs can acquire, hold, and transfer property in India, and any trust structure involving real estate assets must comply with these rules.

NRIs can establish trusts in India and transfer assets into them, but the trust must be structured to comply with both the Indian Trusts Act and FEMA. This typically means appointing at least one trustee who is an Indian resident and domiciled in India.

Tax Implications to Consider

Beyond trusteeship, NRIs setting up Indian private trusts need to navigate several tax considerations. If the same person acts as settlor, trustee, and beneficiary, the trust may be treated as a "revocable trust" — losing its tax and asset protection benefits entirely.

An irrevocable settlement of Indian property into a trust is generally not subject to capital gains tax for individual settlors, regardless of their residential status. However, income generated by trust assets — rental income from property, for instance — is taxable either in the hands of the trustee (as a representative assessee) or directly in the hands of the beneficiaries, depending on whether beneficiary shares are specified in the trust deed.

NRI beneficiaries who are tax residents of India must disclose foreign trust details in their Indian income tax return under Schedule FA.

Practical Steps for NRI Families

For NRIs looking to set up a private trust in India, legal advisors consistently recommend appointing at least one India-resident co-trustee — whether a family member, professional trustee, or trusted associate. The trust deed should clearly specify beneficiaries, their shares, succession plans for trustees, and the process for replacing a trustee who becomes non-resident. Registration with the local registrar, obtaining a PAN for the trust, and ensuring FEMA compliance are all essential steps. Consulting both an Indian trust lawyer and a tax advisor familiar with cross-border implications is not optional — it is necessary.
